newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks testing with California on nuclear dump.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks testing with California on nuclear dump.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Thursday urged California to help it test the safety of the Mojave Desert site where the state wants to build a low-level nuclear waste dump, instead of letting the state conduct the tests by itself.
The administration also urged California Gov. Pete Wilson to drop a lawsuit to try to force the federal government to turn the site over to the state for the proposed Ward Valley nuclear waste dump.

Wilson complained that the Interior Department failed to move ahead on conveying the land, while the state is legally obligated to provide a dump for low-level nuclear waste produced by hospitals, universities and biotechnology companies.

Deputy Interior Secretary John Garamendi in a letter asked California to join forces with the federal government on tests to check whether water could percolate down and carry radioactivity into groundwater near the Colorado River, which supplies drinking water for millions of people.
The offer came after Wilson agreed to more testing at the site, but said the state should perform the tests.
Garamendi in his letter said having the tests conducted by the state and its licensee to operate the proposed facility "will not result in the requisite reliability and objectivity."
A number of environmental groups oppose the Ward Valley plan, fought it in court and pressed for additional environmental tests.
Garamendi said the Energy Department's Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and another competent laboratory should analyse findings, and other experts should review it as well.
The tests involving drilling to determine if tritium, a radioactive gas produced from atomic testing, has seeped down.
"Tritium was not found in measurable amounts in the atmosphere before nuclear tests in the '50s, so it is a timemarker," Garamendi said in a telephone briefing.
